data.key_insight: By inserting all elements into a hash set for O(1) lookups, we can check if an element is the start of a sequence by verifying if `num - 1` is missing from the set. If it is the start, we can count consecutive numbers by checking `num + 1`, `num + 2`, etc.

steps.title: Edge Case Handling
steps.detail: If the input list nums is empty, return 0 immediately.

steps.title: Initialize Hash Set
steps.detail: Convert the list nums into a set called num_set to allow O(1) membership testing and remove duplicates.

steps.title: Find Sequence Starts
steps.detail: Iterate through each number in num_set. For each number, check if (num - 1) is not in num_set. If (num - 1) is absent, this number is the start of a consecutive sequence.

steps.title: Calculate Sequence Length
steps.detail: If it is the start of a sequence, count how many consecutive numbers (num + 1, num + 2, ...) exist in num_set. Keep track of the maximum length found.

events.detail: Pattern: Hash set sequence building · 3 hints

data.pattern_summary: Use a hash set to store all elements for O(1) lookups. Reach for this when you need to find streaks or sequences in an unsorted collection without sorting it first.

pattern_options.name: Sorting
pattern_options.feedback: Sorting the array takes O(n log n) time, which violates the required O(n) time complexity.

pattern_options.name: Hash set sequence building
pattern_options.feedback: Storing elements in a hash set allows O(1) checks for adjacent values, enabling linear time sequence tracking.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Two pointers rely on a sorted array or specific window boundaries, which does not fit an unsorted set of distinct numbers.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic programming
pattern_options.feedback: There is no overlapping subproblem structure here that requires storing intermediate states in a DP table.

signals.hint: Implies looking for unbroken numerical runs like x, x+1, x+2.
Means elements are out of order, so you cannot just scan adjacent indices.

data.brute_force_idea: Iterate through every number in the set, and for each number, continuously check if the next consecutive number exists in the set, counting how far the sequence goes.
data.brute_force_why: In the worst case, for every element, the while loop scans forward through the entire sequence of length n, leading to nested traversal behavior.
data.bottleneck: The inner while loop repeatedly checks for numbers that are part of sequences we have already fully explored or started from elsewhere.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times you start a sequence search from a number that is actually in the middle of a longer sequence.
Ask yourself if you need to check for a sequence starting at x when you already know x - 1 exists.
Think about how to restrict the while loop so it only triggers when you are standing at the absolute beginning of a sequence.

data.overview: The algorithm finds the longest consecutive sequence by using a hash set for O(1) lookups. It only starts counting from numbers that are the beginning of a sequence (i.e., `num - 1` is not in the set), ensuring an O(n) overall time complexity.
data.intuition: Imagine finding the longest chain of consecutive numbered houses on a street. Instead of checking every house, you only check if a house is the first house in a block by looking for its left neighbor; if no left neighbor exists, you walk right counting how far the continuous block goes.

pitfalls: Forgetting to convert the list to a set, which would turn lookups into O(n) and ruin the O(n) time complexity.
Attempting to start sequences from numbers that are not the absolute beginning, causing redundant counting.
Failing to handle empty arrays properly.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force method checks every number as a potential sequence start, repeatedly rescanning the same consecutive streaks from inside out. The optimized solution checks if (num - 1) is present before starting a sequence; if a predecessor exists, num cannot be the start of a streak and is skipped. This guarantees the inner while loop only executes from the genuine starting elements, traversing each number at most once.

derivation.note: Constructing the hash set from the input list processes all n elements.
The loop visits each unique number in the hash set exactly once.
Hash set lookup determines in constant time whether num is the start of a sequence.

derivation.cost: U iterations total across entire loop
derivation.note: Because the loop only triggers on sequence starts, each number is traversed in the while loop at most once overall.
Updates the maximum streak length found so far.

data.time_summary: Building num_set takes O(n) time. The outer loop runs once per unique number, and the inner while loop only runs when num - 1 is absent. Across the entire execution of the algorithm, each number is visited at most twice: once in the outer for loop and at most once inside the while loop. This bounds the total operations to O(n), matching the measured linear growth rate of n^1.06.
data.space_summary: O(n) extra space is used to store up to n unique elements in num_set for O(1) average lookup times.
data.takeaway: To build sequences in unsorted data in O(n) time, store values in a hash set and only initiate forward expansion from true sequence roots (where x - 1 does not exist).
mistakes: Iterating over nums instead of num_set in the outer loop, which causes duplicate work on identical values.
Omitting the (num - 1) not in num_set guard, causing every element to expand sequences and degrading time complexity to O(n^2).
Checking membership in nums instead of num_set, turning each lookup into an O(n) linear scan.
